title: Sum of All Odd Length Subarrays
description: Brute force to optimized: generating every subarray directly versus per-element contribution counting.

blocks.text: Given an array of positive integers arr, calculate the sum of all possible odd-length subarrays, where a subarray's length is the number of elements it contains.

blocks.caption: Count how many odd-length subarrays contain each element, instead of generating every subarray directly

blocks.text: Given an array of positive integers arr, calculate the sum of all possible odd-length subarrays, where a subarray's length is the number of elements it contains.

blocks.title: Analogy: Counting How Many Committees Each Person Joins
blocks.text: Like forming every possible committee of an odd number of consecutive people from a lineup, and instead of tallying each committee's total separately, asking for each person individually: across every committee they could possibly be part of, how many actually have an odd number of members, and adding up their own contribution that many times.

blocks.caption: Instead of tallying each group, ask how many odd-sized groups each person belongs to

blocks.text: With 3 elements, the odd-length subarrays are the three single elements (10, 11, 12) and the one full-length subarray [10, 11, 12], summing to (10+11+12) + 33 = 66.

Before generating every subarray directly, notice that a subarray's sum is nothing more than the sum of its individual elements, and that observation alone suggests a completely different way to organize the same total computation.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The straightforward way to compute this sum is to generate every subarray, check whether its length is odd, and add its own sum to a running total, which correctly answers the question but revisits many of the same elements over and over across different overlapping subarrays.

Observation 2: Every element's final contribution to the grand total is really just that element's own value multiplied by however many odd-length subarrays happen to include it, since a subarray's sum is literally the sum of each of its individual elements.

Observation 3: Swapping the order of summation, from "for each subarray, sum its elements" to "for each element, count how many odd-length subarrays it belongs to", turns the problem into n independent per-element counting questions instead of one big subarray-generation task.

Observation 4: For a specific index i, every subarray containing it is fully determined by choosing how far left the subarray extends, i plus 1 possible starting points, and how far right it extends, n minus i possible ending points; a subarray's total length is odd exactly when this "distance left" and "distance right" share the same parity, both odd or both even, which can be counted directly with simple arithmetic on i and n, no subarray ever generated.

Whenever a total is the sum of an aggregate, like a subarray sum, computed over many overlapping groups, consider swapping the order of summation: compute each individual element's total contribution across every group it belongs to, instead of summing each group separately.

This "swap the order of summation, count each element's contribution directly" technique is broadly reusable whenever a problem asks for a sum-of-sums over many overlapping ranges, and often turns an approach that revisits elements many times into one that touches each element exactly once.

Generate every subarray by choosing a start and an end position, accumulate its sum incrementally as the end position extends, and whenever the resulting length is odd, add that subarray's sum to a running grand total.

items: For every possible starting position, extend the subarray one element at a time, keeping a running sum of the current subarray.
After each extension, check whether the current subarray's length is odd.
If it is, add the current subarray's sum to the overall total.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: current_sum is reset at the start of every new starting position, but then extended incrementally as end grows, avoiding a full resum of the subarray at every single length.
The length is computed directly as end minus start plus 1, checked against odd or even with a simple modulo, since the problem's entire filtering condition depends only on this one value.

Every subarray, odd or even length, is still generated and its running sum maintained, even though only the odd-length ones actually contribute to the total, since skipping the accumulation itself would break the running sum for subsequent, potentially odd-length extensions.

blocks.text: Every possible subarray is generated and its true sum accumulated, so the total is always correct.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), since two nested loops range over all pairs of start and end positions, with O(1) work per pair thanks to the incremental sum.
Space: O(1) extra beyond the loop variables and the running total.

Limitation: this still explicitly visits and processes every one of the roughly n squared over 2 subarrays individually, when each of the n elements could instead have its total contribution computed directly, without ever generating a single subarray at all.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force spends its effort generating and processing every individual subarray, but the same total can be reached from a completely different direction: instead of asking "what is this subarray's sum" for every one of roughly n squared subarrays, ask "how many odd-length subarrays does this element belong to" for just n elements. That count is not arbitrary, it follows directly from where the element sits: a subarray containing index i is fully described by how many elements it includes to the left of i, including i itself, and how many it includes to the right of i, including i itself, and the total length is odd exactly when those two counts share the same parity. Counting how many of the possible left-extensions are odd-sized versus even-sized, and the same for the right-extensions, turns this into simple arithmetic on i and n alone, replacing an entire O(n) inner scan per element with a handful of O(1) calculations.

For each index i, count directly how many odd-length subarrays contain it, without generating any of them. A subarray containing index i is determined by a starting point, one of i plus 1 choices, and an ending point, one of n minus i choices. The subarray's length is odd exactly when the number of choices consumed on the left and on the right share the same parity. Counting how many of the left choices are odd-numbered versus even-numbered, and doing the same for the right choices, gives the total count of odd-length subarrays containing index i directly. Multiplying arr[i] by this count and summing over every index gives the final answer.
For each index, compute directly how many odd-length subarrays contain it, and multiply by that element's value.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Index i","left = i+1, right = n-i","Odd-length subarrays containing i","Contribution","Why"],"rows":[["0","left=1, right=5","3","1 x 3 = 3","Only 1 way to start at or before index 0, and among the 5 ways to end at or after index 0, 3 of those pairings produce an odd total length"],["1","left=2, right=4","4","4 x 4 = 16","With 2 possible starts and 4 possible ends, exactly 4 of the 8 total pairings share matching parity, giving an odd length"],["2","left=3, right=3","5","2 x 5 = 10","The middle index has the most possible subarrays containing it, 3 starts times 3 ends equals 9 total, and 5 of those 9 produce an odd length"],["3","left=4, right=2","4","5 x 4 = 20","Symmetric to index 1, mirrored from the right side of the array"],["4","left=5, right=1","3","3 x 3 = 9","Symmetric to index 0, mirrored from the right side of the array"]]}

codes.python:
def sum_odd_length_subarrays(arr):
    n = len(arr)
    total = 0
    for i in range(n):
        left = i + 1                                              # choices for where the subarray could start
        right = n - i                                                # choices for where the subarray could end
        odd_left = (left + 1) // 2                                     # of those starts, how many keep the total length odd
        even_left = left // 2
        odd_right = (right + 1) // 2
        even_right = right // 2
        count = odd_left * odd_right + even_left * even_right            # total odd-length subarrays containing index i
        total += arr[i] * count                                            # this element's full contribution
    return total


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(sum_odd_length_subarrays([1, 4, 2, 5, 3]))

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), one constant-time calculation per index.
Space: O(1) extra.

Every subarray's own sum is exactly the sum of its individual elements, so summing every odd-length subarray's sum is mathematically identical to summing, for every element, that element's value multiplied by however many odd-length subarrays it happens to appear in; reordering a sum of sums this way never changes its total value, only how it is computed. For a fixed index i, the subarray containing i has length odd exactly when the count of elements from the start through i and the count of elements from i through the end share the same parity, which is precisely what the odd-left-times-odd-right-plus-even-left-times-even-right formula counts directly.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Parity match","What it represents"],"rows":[["Both the left-count and right-count are odd","An odd number of elements on each side of i, including i once, combining to an odd total length"],["Both the left-count and right-count are even","An even number of elements on each side of i, including i once on one side, also combining to an odd total length"]]}

items: left and right directly count how many valid starting points and ending points exist for a subarray containing index i, without ever constructing any of those subarrays.
The odd and even splits of those two counts use simple integer division, separating how many represent an odd distance versus an even distance from index i.
The parity-matching formula, odd-left times odd-right plus even-left times even-right, gives the exact number of odd-length subarrays containing index i in constant time.

Adding arr[i] times that count directly accumulates this one element's full contribution across every odd-length subarray it belongs to, all in a single step, with no subarray ever explicitly generated or summed.

blocks.text: This problem is a clean showcase of the "swap the order of summation, count each element's contribution" technique: instead of summing many overlapping groups directly, compute how much each individual element contributes across all of them, then sum those individual contributions instead.

items: Trying to directly track a running count of odd-length subarrays while sliding a window, instead of recognizing that each index's total contribution can be computed independently and directly from its own position alone.

Getting the parity-matching formula backwards, such as pairing odd-left with even-right instead of matching odd with odd and even with even, which produces the count of even-length subarrays instead of odd-length ones.
Forgetting to multiply the final count by arr[i] itself, and instead just summing the counts, which would count subarrays instead of computing the actual total sum being asked for.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["A single element array","Has exactly one subarray, of length 1, always odd, so the answer is simply that one element's own value"],["Every element identical","The technique still applies unchanged, since the counting formula depends only on position and length, never on the actual values themselves"]]}

items: Introduce the "sum of sums, so swap the summation order and count each element's contribution" framing explicitly and early, since deriving the parity-matching formula from first principles, rather than presenting it as a memorized formula, is what demonstrates real understanding here.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Sum some aggregate, like a subarray sum, over every one of many overlapping groups" points toward swapping the order of summation: compute each individual element's total contribution across every group it belongs to, instead of summing each group separately.

items: How would this change if you needed the sum of all even-length subarrays instead? Swap which parity pairing is counted, matching odd-left with even-right and even-left with odd-right instead, since that is exactly the complementary count.

What if you needed the count of odd-length subarrays with a sum greater than some threshold, not just the total sum? The per-element contribution trick no longer directly applies, since that condition depends on the actual values within each subarray, not just its length and position; a different technique, potentially involving prefix sums and a sorted structure, would be needed.

How would you verify this contribution-counting formula is correct without just trusting it? Compare its output against the brute force approach on several small examples, and separately, algebraically confirm that summing count(i) times arr[i] for a tiny fixed array by hand matches directly listing every odd-length subarray's sum.

The classic example of the "swap summation order, count each element's contribution across overlapping groups" technique, also useful in problems summing subarray minimums, maximums, or other aggregate properties across every subarray.

Same "position relative to both ends of the array determines a count directly, with no explicit enumeration" reasoning as Find the Highest Altitude's prefix-based tracking, though applied here to a combinatorial count instead of a running total.
Same general "reduce a quadratic or worse enumeration to a linear per-element formula" progression seen throughout the prefix-sum and combinatorics-heavy problems in this category.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(1) extra space.
Optimized (per-element contribution counting): O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: Per-element contribution counting, swapping the order of summation from "per subarray" to "per element"

Core Idea: Instead of summing every odd-length subarray directly, compute how many odd-length subarrays contain each individual element, using a simple parity-matching formula based only on that element's position and the array's length
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: A sum over many overlapping groups can often be computed faster by summing each element's total contribution across all groups instead of summing each group separately
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Count how many odd-length subarrays each element belongs to, do not generate the subarrays themselves
